rv.q: As embodied by a brilliant Ethan Hawke, in full-menace mode, and a tightly wired Paul Dano, everyday sibling rivalry has seldom felt this ominous.
The production, directed by James Macdonald, is a master class in how to stage Shepard's volatile family drama
Shepard’s play is symbolic and strange, if also a bit thin.
Hawke, of course, lives for this type of juicy role, playing dirty in more ways than one.
But up inside its jewel box, so neatly delineated and so separate from us, the mess this production makes is largely artificial, well designed but not dangerous.
It’s a sign of Shepard’s generosity that the two other roles offer actors plenty to get their teeth into.
In other words, this is the most well-behaved True West I’ve ever seen.
But it works marvelously as a mood piece, which for several reasons this production only partially succeeds in capturing.
Ethan Hawke and Paul Dano duke it out as battling brothers in a disappointing revival of Sam Shepard’s fierce 1980 classic.

For this production, the Roundabout, under James Macdonald’s direction, has brought together Ethan Hawke and Paul Dano, who somehow produce all the great upheaval of a 10-gallon hat left out in a drizzle.

Shepard�s True West is not of that caliber. You can anticipate wonderfully low key, well paced, and completely absorbing performances. Hoffman and Reilly, regardless of the role each is playing at the moment, transcend the limits of this production, and make True West one of the few �must see� plays of this season.
But while watching them go at it is entertaining, what the play is fighting for isn’t as clear.
In elder brother Lee, a drifter and thief, Hawke has found a vehicle for both his comedic facility (not always mined or guided adroitly, on stage or screen) and his capacity for menace.

The play, about a pair of estranged brothers and their apparent role reversal under pressure, is as funny as it is serious, and this new staging, directed by James Macdonald, a specialist in heavy-hitters, is as entertaining as it is profound.
Hawke and Dano aren’t even distant cousins.
This new version, directed by James Macdonald, could use a high-voltage power infusion.
People will go to see Ethan Hawke, and there are moments when he does not disappoint.
But star-power short-circuits in this curiously light-hearted production from director James Macdonald at the Theatre.

cn.t: Critics praise Hawke and Dano's performances in this Shepard revival, though responses are mixed on the production itself. Some find it a "ripping," "blazing" showcase, while others deem it tedious and question whether the play still resonates.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
